transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-02-25
Time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (Pelican CTO), Aisha Khan (Pelican Infra Lead), Ben Yeo (Pelican ML Eng)

Summary (auto): deep dive on p95/p99 tail latency; discussion of streaming vs chunked responses, KV cache behavior with long prefix contexts, batching strategies, quantization impacts; network hops for Pelican's VPC peering were discussed; agreed next steps and pilot scope.

[00:00] Jordan: ok everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood, and Samira the SE is here with me. quick roll call?
[00:10] Carlos: hey Jordan, Carlos here, Aisha and Ben on my side.
[00:15] Aisha: Aisha, infra.
[00:18] Ben: Ben, ML.
[00:20] Samira: thanks folks. high level goal for today is to understand your p95/p99 pain, and talk through KV cache, batching, streaming tradeoffs and network hops for your VPC peering setup.
[00:32] Jordan: we'll try to keep it practical, and leave time for the pilot steps at the end.

[02:05] Carlos: quick context — our prod LLM is a 13B variant, serving mixed workloads: short completions (~100 tokens) and long-context assistants up to 8k tokens. p95 is usually ok, around 120ms for short, but p99 tail spikes have been causing timeouts for some interactive flows. we saw worst cases 1.2s or worse which trips our frontend.
[02:31] Ben: and we do a lot of streaming responses client-side, but some routes are non-streamed for post-processing. tail seems worse on non-streaming endpoints, maybe because of batching?

[04:00] Samira: makes sense. one thing to flag: streaming has incremental flushes so perceived latency is often lower even if total compute is same. non-streaming aggregates end-to-end and exposes tail from the slowest token. but let's step through architecture: are you running Redwood Dedicated or private?
[04:25] Carlos: currently evaluating Dedicated. we'd likely run in a VPC peered region to avoid public egress, so network hops include our internal LB -> peering -> Redwood nodes -> back. Aisha has a diagram.
[04:40] Aisha: yes — there's NAT at our side for certain services, and we're also using a managed firewall which adds a couple of micro hops. we measured 8-12ms RTT to the Redwood region from our cluster.

[06:12] Samira: ok that RTT is fine, but tail can still be dominated by first-token kernel startup, KV cache misses, and head-room in batching queue. two broad levers: reduce variance at the runtime (fast kernels, warm KV cache), and reduce queueing variance (batching policy and priority routing).
[06:45] Jordan: wanted to bring up that we instrument per-token CPU/GPU times and queue wait times in the console — we can share the traces.

[08:00] Ben: we've seen a pattern where long-context requests that scroll through large prefixes cause KV cache thrash when users jump to a different conversation. can you explain warm vs cold KV cache behavior?
[08:20] Samira: sure — the runtime keeps per-request KV caches for the sequence. when a new request arrives with a prefix that's been recently served, we can reuse cached keys which drops transformer attention compute. a cold miss forces recomputation and memory loads, increasing per-token latency by a factor. with long prefixes, the working set can exceed cache, causing eviction.
[09:05] Ben: is that deterministic based on token count or sequence diversity?
[09:15] Samira: both. token count affects size; sequence diversity affects reuse. if many unique conversations are interleaved on the same GPU, hit rate falls. solution is customer-side routing (sticky sessions), larger KV cache config, or pinning workloads to dedicated pools.

[11:40] Aisha: for Dedicated we'd like to avoid warm-up jitter on traffic bursts. any recommended warmup patterns?
[11:55] Samira: synthetic warmers that replay representative prefixes at low QPS before traffic ramp; also background prefetching of likely KV segments for known high-volume conversations. we also support keeping pinned warmed replicas during launch window.

[13:30] Jordan: let's talk numbers — p95 vs p99. our internal benchmarks show p95 for 13B on A100-ish hardware with streaming is ~90-150ms for short outputs, p99 can be 3-6x that depending on cache and queueing. in non-streaming flows p99 often amplifies because mistake or slow token stalls push the last-token latency out.
[14:05] Carlos: that's consistent. one question — how much of p99 is network vs compute?
[14:18] Samira: depends. for you with 8-12ms RTT, network is small but not negligible. take example: 8ms outbound + 8ms inbound = 16ms base. if streaming, you get partial tokens earlier. But compute tail from kernel and KV miss can add 200-800ms. traces we ask for will break it down into network, queue, compute, and de-serialize times.

[16:50] Ben: about batching: we currently do dynamic batching in our infra; curious how Redwood's continuous batching works and whether it increases tail.
[17:05] Samira: our runtime supports continuous batching which aggregates tokens across requests and uses a time-slicing policy — we aim to minimize queue wait while keeping GPU saturation. dynamic batch sizes are used; worst-case tail can increase if a single long request blocks smaller short ones in naive implementations. our scheduler supports priority lanes: low-latency lanes for short interactive requests and bulk lanes for high throughput. you can configure lane sizes and max wait thresholds.
[18:10] Carlos: can you give an example config for mixed workloads?
[18:20] Samira: yes — typical config: low-latency lane with max wait 12ms, max batch 8 tokens; bulk lane max wait 60ms, batch up to GPU capacity. that reduces p99 for interactive flows while preserving throughput. We'll share a recommended policy tuned for your QPS mix.

[20:00] Aisha: on quantization — we ran 4-bit quant and saw slight accuracy drift. Does quantization impact token latency significantly?
[20:15] Samira: quantization helps compute latency by fitting more of the model on-chip and reducing memory transfers; for A100-like GPUs, int8/4-bit kernels reduce per-token compute by ~15-40% depending on kernel. but there's also kernel variance — some quantized kernels are newer and show more variance at the tails due to memory access patterns. we recommend running evals on your prompts; we'll include quality vs latency curves in the bench sheet.

[22:40] Ben: regarding streaming vs non-streaming, if we switch to always-stream would that hide tail without reducing cost?
[22:55] Samira: streaming changes perceived latency but not total compute cost. It amortizes early tokens so users get partial output earlier; however, last-token p99 still exists and can affect correctness if client retries or there's an end-of-stream dependency. For cost, same tokens. For p99-sensitive UX, prefer streaming with progressive validation and server-side retries if a token miss happens.

[25:30] Jordan: bringing up network hops again — Aisha mentioned NAT and managed firewall. those middle hops can add jitter. do you capture jitter in your monitoring?
[25:45] Aisha: we have ping distributions but not per-request tracing into vendor endpoints.
[25:50] Samira: we recommend end-to-end distributed tracing enabled on both sides — we'll share a tracing header to propagate through requests. that will let you see exact hop times. also MTU path MTU issues can cause fragmentation for large streaming frames; we suggest adjusting max chunk size if you see retransmits.

[28:10] Carlos: any tips for preventing head-of-line blocking with long token sequences?
[28:25] Samira: implement priority lanes and preemptible small batches; also consider chunking long responses into smaller logical interactions so they don't monopolize per-GPU scheduling. KV-aware routing helps: route long conversational streams to separate pinned machines so short interactive queries remain unaffected.

[32:00] Ben: curious about fallback strategies in case of cluster overload — do you provide model variant fallbacks?
[32:10] Jordan: yes, smart routing can fallback to a smaller model variant or lower-precision variant. policy can be time-based or queue-depth-based. we also support multi-variant A/B rollouts and automatic fallback when latency breaches SLO.

[34:20] Carlos: we need to ensure no PII leaves box — on Dedicated, can you ensure KMS in our VPC?
[34:35] Samira: Dedicated offers customer-managed KMS and options for VPC-only private endpoints; we can also arrange on-prem package if you need air-gapped. security docs will be in the package Jordan sends.

[36:50] Aisha: ok let's walk through a concrete benchmark you suggested earlier. what do you need from us to reproduce our p99?
[37:05] Samira: we need: representative prompts (4k and 8k prefixes), QPS mix, client-side streaming settings (frame size), average token length, and your VPC network diagram. we'll run two runs: streaming-enabled and non-streaming to compare p95/p99 and breakdowns.

[40:10] Ben: how long will a bench run take and how many requests?
[40:20] Samira: typical bench is 30-90 minutes depending on variance; we'll run multiple windows to capture tail and warm caches. you'll get raw traces and aggregated p50/p95/p99 plus component breakdowns.

[42:00] Jordan: touching on cost — sometimes customers over-tune for p99 and sacrifice unit economics. we can help find a middle-ground with batching/quantization and dedicated burst options.

[44:30] Carlos: regarding observability, can we get token-level timing in the console and per-route dashboards?
[44:42] Samira: yes, per-route dashboards exist and you can enable token-level breakdown with a small overhead. we also export traces via OTLP and logs to your logging endpoint.

[47:10] Aisha: for the pilot, can we pin a small Dedicated pool to replicate our QPS?
[47:18] Jordan: yes — typical pilot is 1-2 devices sized to match your peak concurrency; we'll recommend instance type after we see your workload.

[50:00] Ben: one more thing — we've seen GC/host-side jitter when other jobs run on same landlord host. does Redwood isolate at the GPU level?
[50:12] Samira: yes, workloads are pinned to GPU devices; we also have tenant-aware cgroups and OOM protection. for Dedicated we guarantee no noisy neighbor on the same GPU devices. host-level system jobs can still cause minor jitter, but we monitor and auto-remediate.

[53:30] Jordan: quick recap before we move to logistics: 1) Redwood to run p95/p99 bench with and without streaming; 2) Samira to run KV-cache microbench; 3) Pelican to share prompts, traffic distribution, and network topology; 4) Jordan to send security and Dedicated pricing. agreed?
[53:50] Carlos: agreed.
[54:05] Aisha: agreed.

[54:30] Jordan: OK last bits — any concerns about fallbacks and data residency?
[54:38] Carlos: just the KMS and audit logs — we need evidence of key handling policies.
[54:44] Samira: we'll include SOC2 summary, KMS reference, and sample audit logs in the security bundle.

[58:00] Ben: small nit — you mentioned prefetching KV segments. how do you avoid prefetch blowing up memory?
[58:10] Samira: prefetch is heuristic and rate-limited; we use LRU and predictive models that only prefetch for high-confidence sequences. it's configurable per-tenant.

[60:50] Carlos: timeline for pilot?
[60:58] Jordan: if we get artifacts this week, pilot can start target week of 2026-03-09; two-week pilot to gather tail metrics.

[65:15] Aisha: ok thanks — we'll aim to share prompt set and topology by 2026-03-01.
[65:25] Jordan: perfect. we'll follow up with a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff and share the bench template.

[70:00] Ben: thanks everyone, this was useful.
[70:05] Carlos: thanks.
[70:08] Samira: thanks, bye.

Action Items referenced above. Links shared: "benchmark spreadsheet (link)"; "security bundle (link)"; "pilot kickoff invite (calendar link)"
